article:
**After the betting-adjacent boom, IPL cricket is becoming a shopping mall, chat room and ad machine**

The most revealing IPL technology story of 2026 was not another billionaire franchise deal or a breathless comparison with the NFL. It was the quiet disappearance of a familiar match-night ritual: millions of fans opening fantasy apps, paying to enter contests, and watching every wicket as both sport and personal financial event.

That part of Indian cricket’s mobile economy was abruptly broken in August 2025, when India enacted the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act. The law bans online money games across chance, skill and mixed formats, and also prohibits advertising and payment facilitation for them. The government justified the move by saying such platforms had affected about 45 crore people and caused losses exceeding ₹20,000 crore — figures that should be treated as official claims, not independently verified counts. ([pib.gov.in](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressNoteDetails.aspx?ModuleId=3&NoteId=158400&lang=3&reg=3))

What has emerged since is not a retreat from digital cricket. It is a redesign of it.

The IPL’s mobile-first ecosystem is moving from fantasy-money products toward a more intricate stack: streaming platforms that know what people watch, ad systems that segment them into cohorts, commerce integrations that nudge them to order food during play, AI search tools that turn cricket curiosity into platform engagement, and creator-led watch parties that try to keep fans talking inside company-owned apps.

The podcast claim that the IPL may be on track to surpass the NFL as the world’s most valuable sports league is too broad to carry the story. On media rights alone, the NFL remains in another category: its long-term U.S. distribution agreements run through the 2033 season and are worth more than $100 billion by reported estimates. The IPL’s 2023-2027 media rights, while enormous, were sold by the BCCI for ₹48,390.32 crore — roughly $6 billion at recent exchange rates. ([nfl.com](https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-completes-long-term-media-distribution-agreements-through-2033-season?utm_source=openai))

But that comparison misses what is actually new. The IPL has become India’s live laboratory for what sport looks like when the television broadcast, phone screen, influencer economy, digital advertising market and consumer payments stack all converge.

The structure for that convergence was already in place. The BCCI split IPL rights for 2023-2027, with television and digital rights sold separately. After Reliance and Disney combined their Indian media assets, the Competition Commission of India noted that the merged parties would hold television and digital rights for major live cricket events, including IPL tournaments, until 2027. The regulator also observed that cricket is not treated by broadcasters as interchangeable with other sports in India, and warned that the combined entity could gain stronger negotiating power over subscriptions and advertising. ([images.assettype.com](https://images.assettype.com/barandbench/2024-10-23/s0gln04k/Viacom18_Disney_Hotstar_CCI_order.pdf))

That regulatory language can sound abstract. For an ordinary fan, it means the phone is no longer just the place where the match appears. It is where the surrounding economy happens.

JioHotstar, the unified streaming platform created after the Reliance-Disney India merger, says it had 450 million monthly average users as of April 2026 and offers content in 19 languages. Its parent’s annual report says IPL 2026’s opening weekend reached more than 515 million viewers across TV and digital. The same report describes the platform’s strategic focus as “improving monetisation and platform excellence,” including better personalisation and sharper audience targeting. ([jiostar.com](https://www.jiostar.com/news/jiohotstar-launches-industry-first-commerce-signal-led-advertising-to-power-intent-driven-engagement-at-scale/))

That is the language of a media platform, not just a broadcaster.

JioHotstar’s own advertising materials show how granular the match-night economy is becoming. Its self-serve ad platform offers more than 1,000 pre-built audience cohorts, campaign forecasting, reporting dashboards, video and display ads, and trial rates listed at ₹75 CPM for video and ₹45 CPM for display on entertainment content, with budgets starting at ₹50,000. ([ads.hotstar.com](https://ads.hotstar.com/))

In April 2026, JioHotstar launched what it called “signal-led commerce advertising” with Instamart. The company described it as a way for brands to reach audiences based on intent signals inside a premium streaming environment, including during marquee events like the Tata IPL. In plain terms: while the viewer watches cricket, the platform can help advertisers identify when the viewer may be ready to buy. ([jiostar.com](https://www.jiostar.com/news/jiohotstar-launches-industry-first-commerce-signal-led-advertising-to-power-intent-driven-engagement-at-scale/))

There is a human shift inside this technical one. The earlier fantasy-sports boom invited fans to feel like managers, analysts and gamblers-adjacent participants in the match. The new model invites them to become viewers, data profiles, shoppers, commenters and followers of creators.

Dream11’s pivot makes that change visible. Before the ban, Dream Sports said real-money gaming accounted for about 95% of its business. After the law, the company told Fortune India it would not lay off employees and would rebuild around AI and the creator economy. By December 2025, Dream11 announced a formal pivot from gaming to a “second-screen sports entertainment platform,” with creator-led watch-alongs, real-time banter, bite-sized sports moments and free-to-play fantasy sports. ([fortuneindia.com](https://www.fortuneindia.com/business-news/dream11-parent-wont-lay-off-any-of-its-employees-ready-to-rebuild-from-the-ground-up-harsh-jain/125964))

Harsh Jain, Dream11 and Dream Sports co-founder and CEO, framed the pivot as social rather than financial: “No sports fan should ever watch a match alone,” he said in the company announcement. That is a warm promise. It is also a business model. The new Dream11 keeps the fan’s second screen active during live sport, but changes the source of monetisation from entry fees and winnings to advertising, sponsorships, creator activity and platform engagement. ([dreamsports.group](https://www.dreamsports.group/media-and-blog/dream11-pivots-from-gaming-to-a-sports-entertainment-platform))

The transition has not been painless. In April 2026, The Economic Times reported that more than 100 executives had left Dream Sports after restructuring, with departures from customer support, engineering and data functions. A company spokesperson said Dream11’s 700 employees had been placed into new startup-like units and that around 15% chose to leave. The same report said other real-money gaming firms had reduced headcount more sharply after the ban. ([economictimes.indiatimes.com](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/tech/technology/rmg-ban-hit-dream-sports-rejigs-operations-as-over-100-executives-check-out/articleshow/129474986.cms?UTM_Campaign=RSS_Feed&UTM_Medium=Referral&UTM_Source=Google_Newsstand))

So the IPL’s technology story now has two very different human consequences.

For people harmed by compulsive money gaming, the ban may have removed a dangerous financial layer from match nights. The government explicitly cited financial, psychological and social harms in justifying the law. But for workers who built the fantasy-sports economy, the same decision turned stable product roadmaps into emergency pivots. And for fans, the match did not become less commercial. It became commercial in a different way.

The old fantasy app asked: can you predict the players better than other fans? The new platform economy asks: can you be kept watching, chatting, ordering, clicking and returning?

That does not make the new model inherently worse. A watch-along can be less financially risky than a paid fantasy contest. A regional-language mobile stream can make cricket more accessible than a cable bundle. A self-serve ad platform may let smaller brands buy IPL-adjacent attention once reserved for national advertisers.

But the dignity question is still there: when a fan opens an IPL stream, are they being served cricket — or converted into a constantly measurable consumer event?

That is the overlooked story. The IPL is not simply becoming “more valuable.” It is becoming a platform economy in which the fan’s attention is sliced into advertising cohorts, commerce opportunities and creator interactions. The post-ban era did not end the business of monetising cricket emotion. It changed who gets paid, who gets watched, and what ordinary fans are being asked to give in return.
